summary: This best current practice documents the syntax used in YANG module tree diagrams, the compact text pictures of a module's structure. It gathers the definition in one place so authors and readers can interpret the diagrams consistently. The syntax may be updated over time as YANG evolves.

plainLanguage.summary: A family tree shows who is related to whom in a small picture. This explains how to read the little text pictures that show the shape of network configuration data.

subtitle: The single reference for the text notation used to draw the shape of a YANG module.

tldr.problem: Documents that show a YANG module as a tree diagram each had to re-explain the diagram syntax, which was repeated and could drift apart.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8340 defines the symbols once: a directory-listing style tree where each node is printed as status, flags, name, options, type and features, plus rules for groupings, mount points and long diagrams.
tldr.outcome: Authors can cite one document instead of redefining the notation, and the syntax can be updated in one place as YANG evolves. It is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 8791.

today: RFC 8340 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 215) and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8791. Its text says the syntax may be updated or replaced as the YANG language changes.

sections.title: Why a Shared Definition
sections.content:
YANG tree diagrams were first published in RFC 6536. They give a simplified picture of a data model and can be generated by tools such as pyang.

Until now it was common practice to repeat the definition of the syntax in every document that included a tree diagram. RFC 8340 says this has disadvantages and instead gathers the definition in a single place. It does not intend to restrict future changes, only to make sure changes are easily identified and agreed. The document expects to be updated or replaced as the YANG language (RFC 7950) changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every book explaining the same map symbols again, there is now one legend that everyone can point to.

sections.title: Tree Diagram Layout
sections.content:
A full tree diagram starts with module: and the module name. It then has sections in a fixed order: top-level data nodes, augmentations, RPCs, notifications, groupings and yang-data structures. Each section is offset by two spaces.

The layout looks like the output of a file-system directory listing. Each node starts with +--, child nodes are offset from their parent by three spaces, and siblings that are separated by other lines are linked with a vertical bar (|).

Submodules are drawn the same way but begin with submodule:. Groupings can be shown expanded, as if the nodes were defined where the uses statement is, or unexpanded, printing only the grouping name. Sibling nodes can be collapsed with ..., and single-line comments start with //.
sections.plainLanguage: It looks like the folder list on a computer: each item hangs off the one above it, pushed a little to the right, with lines to show which items are neighbors.

sections.title: How Each Node Is Printed
sections.content:
Every node is printed as <status>--<flags> <name><opts> <type> <if-features>.

  • Status: + for current, x for deprecated, o for obsolete.
  • Flags: rw for configuration data nodes and choice nodes, ro for non-configuration data, rpc and action output and notification parameters, -w for input parameters, -u for uses of a grouping, -x for rpcs and actions, -n for notifications, and mp for nodes with a mount-point extension. Case nodes have no flags.
  • Name: (name) marks a choice node and :(name) a case node. A node augmented in from another module is printed as prefix:name.
  • Options: ? for an optional leaf, choice, anydata or anyxml, ! for a presence container, an asterisk after the name for a leaf-list or list, [keys] for a list's keys, / for a top-level node in a mounted module and @ for a top-level node of a module named in a mount point parent reference.
  • Type: the type name for leafs and leaf-lists. A leafref is printed as -> TARGET or as leafref.
  • If-features: the features the node depends on, written {...}?.

Extra whitespace between fields is allowed, for example to align columns.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line is like a label on a box: one symbol says whether it is old or new, another says whether you can change it or only look, and the rest give its name and what kind of thing it holds.

sections.title: Guidelines for Using Diagrams in RFCs
sections.content:
RFCs and Internet-Drafts limit lines to 72 characters. A longer node line should be broken between the options and the type, or between the type and the if-feature, and indented to start below the name with at least two spaces. Long paths such as leafref paths or augment targets may also be split over several lines. For a figure in a document, --tree-line-length 69 works well with pyang.

If a module consists only of groupings, its diagram should show the groupings. Diagrams are meant to be a simplified view, so diagrams longer than a page should generally be avoided. A long diagram can be split into several smaller ones, for example one for data nodes and another for notifications, or one per subtree. Authors should also consider whether a long diagram belongs in an appendix.
sections.plainLanguage: If a picture is too wide or too tall for the page, you cut it into smaller pictures, and you make sure each line still fits on the paper.

sections.title: Schema Mount Diagrams
sections.content:
YANG schema mount lets one or more modules be mounted at a mount point of another schema. Any container or list can be a mount point, and it is marked in the module with the mount-point extension. In a tree diagram the node gets the mp flag.

Which modules actually appear under a mount point is controlled by the server, so a diagram of mounted modules treats the mount point much like a container that uses a grouping. Top-level nodes of a mounted module are shown with / and those reachable by parent reference with @. Whether mounted data is configuration or not comes from the config leaf in the schema mount module, and the flags (rw or ro) follow it.

The RFC notes that a module that augments a mounted one, such as ietf-ospf augmenting ietf-routing, has no special mount-related notation.
sections.plainLanguage: A mount point is like a slot in a toy where you can snap in another piece. The diagram marks the slot and then shows whichever pieces were snapped in.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC states that there is no security impact related to the tree diagrams it defines, and that it has no IANA actions. The diagrams are documentation notation, not a protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a way of drawing a picture, so there is nothing here that anyone could break into.

data.title: Interfaces tree
data.code:
+--rw interfaces
   +--rw interface* [name]
      +--rw name                        string
      +--rw description?                string
      +--rw type                        identityref
      +--rw enabled?                    boolean
      +--rw link-up-down-trap-enable?   enumeration {if-mib}?
